headline: Nine Days Running: The Hudson's Warm Edge Refuses to Break
subhead: The filament that's carried the canyon bite through August is still sitting on the wall heading into Labor Day week — here's how long it can last.
body_markdown:
Ninety fathoms to better than a thousand in under three miles — that's the drop along the east wall by the Claw, and it's exactly the kind of structure that holds a temperature break in place once one sets up on it. That break has been sitting there for the better part of nine days now, and as of this week it still hasn't moved. That's the whole story of the Hudson right now. We flagged this pattern last week — said the setup would hold through several more days of stable high pressure before any wind shift or cool front started pushing on that warm edge — and that's precisely what's happened. No front has come through strong enough to knock it loose, and the fleet running out of Shinnecock, Manasquan, and Jones has been cashing in on it.

What's holding this together is a Gulf Stream filament that's kept warm water pinned against the canyon wall since mid-August, and it's doing what these filaments do best — pushing bait up against the 100-fathom line and stacking it there instead of letting it scatter into open water. That's the difference between a mixed week and a week where boats are running lines out before the sun's fully up. The color along the edge has stayed clean blue where the filament sits, with the dirtier green water pushed well up onto the shelf, and that contrast is as good a visual cue as any SST chart — if you're running out and the water goes from green to that deep cobalt blue somewhere around the Dip, you've found the edge worth working.

Yellowfin have been the most consistent player all week, showing on the troll in that 60- to 100-fathom stretch off the Claw, mixed in with a scattering of small bigeye that are pushing the average size up on some boats. Green machines and cedar plugs in the smaller spread positions have been drawing strikes on the troll, with naked ballyhoo and horse ballyhoo skirted in blue-white and green-machine combos working the long riggers. Boats willing to slow-troll or drift-chunk butterfish after dark over structure near the canyon head have reported better-grade bigeye mixed in with the yellowfin, which tracks with what's typically expected once the filament has had time to concentrate bait for over a week straight — the bigger fish move up onto the structure once the small stuff is reliably stacked there.

Wahoo have been a bonus rather than a target this week, mostly picked off on high-speed presentations — bombers and Ilanders pulled at 12 to 15 knots through the temperature seam itself, right where the warm and cooler water meet along the wall. That seam is narrow, sometimes only a quarter mile wide, so it takes discipline to stay on it rather than run through it. Mahi have been scattered around any floating structure or weed lines found drifting near the Dip, mostly schoolie-sized fish in the 3- to 8-pound class, but worth a few minutes with light spinning gear and small skirted jigs if the trolling bite goes quiet for a stretch. White marlin sightings have picked up on the troll as well, mostly incidental with the tuna spread, and a few boats have swaped one long rigger over to a naked ballyhoo on a lighter leader once a marlin's been spotted working the spread — worth having that rod rigged and ready rather than trying to re-rig on the fly.

The deep-drop swordfish game during daylight hours remains a long-day proposition this time of year, and with the bait and structure situation holding the way it has, boats making that run have generally had better luck staying patient on one drop over the canyon structure rather than moving around chasing marks. It's not a numbers game right now so much as a quality one — one good bite on a well-placed drop beats three shallow marks worked halfway.

The next several days should look a lot like the last several, provided the pattern holds. High pressure has been the stabilizing force here, and as long as it stays put, there's no reason for that warm filament to break down or slide off the wall. The one thing worth watching closely is the calendar — this is peak hurricane season, and any tropical development spinning up in the western Atlantic is the single biggest threat to this setup. A storm track that pushes swell and wind into the Bight would mix that warm water down and scatter the bait that's currently stacked along the edge, and it wouldn't take much to undo nine days of a good pattern. Keep an eye on storm tracks through the week rather than just the local forecast — that's the bigger variable right now.

If the pattern holds through the weekend, the play is the same one that's worked all week: run to the temperature seam along the wall near the Claw or the Dip, work the troll early with a green-machine and ballyhoo spread, and be ready to switch to chunking butterfish if the bite goes quiet midday. If a front does start pushing through and the edge starts to break down, don't be surprised if the bite gets patchier and more mark-dependent rather than the wide-open structure-following pattern it's been. Either way, this filament has already outlasted expectations for early September — worth taking advantage of it while it's still sitting where it is.
